```{r}
bank <- read.csv("UniversalBank.csv")
print("Bank Dims")
dim(bank) #5000 rows, 14 cols
#strip data to reqs.
bank <- bank[, c("Online", "CreditCard", "Personal.Loan")]
#rename for ease.
names(bank) <- c("Online", "CC", "Loan")
#factors for y/n binary
bank$Online <- factor(bank$Online, levels = c(0,1))
bank$CC <- factor(bank$CC, levels = c(0,1))
bank$Loan <- factor(bank$Loan, levels = c(0,1))
#check
print("Bank Loan Table")
table(bank$Loan)
```

```{r}
#partition for training
set.seed(1234567890)
split <- sample(seq_len(nrow(bank)), size=round(0.6*nrow(bank)))
training <- bank[split,]
validation <- bank[-split,]
#check each && validate
nrow(training)
nrow(validation)
#compare rows of each sum to original data rows for quick test
if (nrow(training) + nrow(validation) != nrow(bank)) {
  print("ERROR: Training + Validation != Bank rows")
}
```
## Part A - Pivot Table {R via ftable}
```{r}
#pivot table. basic r, not w/ reshape2.
PtA <- table(CC=training$CC, Loan=training$Loan, Online = training$Online)
ftable(PtA, row.vars = c("CC", "Loan"), col.vars="Online")
```

## Part B - Classifying Cust actively using / acceptance?

Probability is 9.85% (rounded).
^{Note this would change with seed}.
```{r}
PtB_accept <- PtA["1", "1", "1"] #loan acceptance
PtB_decline <- PtA["1", "0", "1"] #loan decline
PtB_prob <- PtB_accept / (PtB_accept + PtB_decline)
round(PtB_prob, 4) 
```

## Part C - Two tables loans as f(online) && loans as f(cc)
```{r}
#rows x online
tLoanOnline <- table(Loan = training$Loan, Online = training$Online)
#r-c summaries to check
addmargins(tLoanOnline)
#rows x cc
tLoanCC <- table(Loan = training$Loan, CC = training$CC)
addmargins(tLoanCC)

```

## Part D - Compute Con/Marg probs
```{r}
#props as p. margin1 row sums to 1; p(pred|loan)
pOnline <- prop.table(tLoanOnline, margin=1)
pCC <- prop.table(tLoanCC, margin=1)
#loan shares of training = priors (p(loan 0), p(loan 1)
pLoan <- prop.table(table(training$Loan))
#r/c=loan/pred
PtD_prob <- c(
  "P(CC=1 | Loan=1)"     = pCC["1", "1"],
  "P(Online=1 | Loan=1)" = pOnline["1", "1"],
  "P(Loan=1)"            = pLoan[["1"]],
  "P(CC=1 | Loan=0)"     = pCC["0", "1"],
  "P(Online=1 | Loan=0)" = pOnline["0", "1"],
  "P(Loan=0)"            = pLoan[["0"]]
)
round(PtD_prob, 4)
```

## Part E - Naive Bayes
```{r}
#product loan=1 [1:3] vs loan=0 [4:6] -- normalize
#i think this would have been more fun with linear algebra tho
#turning D probs to matrix & exp(log(matr) %*% rep(1,3))
nYes <- prod(PtD_prob[1:3])
nNo <- prod(PtD_prob[4:6])
PtE_prob <- nYes / (nYes+nNo)
round(PtE_prob, 4)
```

## Part F - Compare values
```
Diff&Ratio to compare values.
PartB is higher probability of acceptance by .0279%
PartB is higher ratio by .284%
None of these values classify beyond the threshhold of 0.5, so it does not 
impact our sample cust.
The value in PtB is more accurate as it only uses matching records.
No independence assumption is made via PtB method. 
PtE  uses all records & assumes cc/online are independent, given loan.
```

```{r}
#gap between estimates, in percentage points
PtF_diff <- (PtB_prob - PtE_prob) * 100
round(PtF_diff, 4)
#relative gap: how much higher B's estimate is than E's, in %
PtF_ratio <- (PtB_prob / PtE_prob - 1) * 100
round(PtF_ratio, 3)
```

## Part G - naiveBayes() model output vs Part E
```
Entries for P(Loan=1 | CC=1, Online=1): only the six PtD values.
Loan x CC table: the CC=1 column, both Loan rows.
Loan x Online table: Online=1 column, both Loan rows.
Loan row totals, giving P(Loan=1) and P(Loan=0).
The CC=0 and Online=0 columns are not needed for this customer.
```

```{r}
#fit nb on training; factors -> categorical tables (laplace=0 default, no smoothing)
PtG_model <- naiveBayes(Loan ~ CC + Online, data = training)
#a-priori = p(loan); conditional tables: rows = loan, cols = predictor level
PtG_model
#cust profile: cc=1, online=1 (levels must match training factors)
PtG_cust <- data.frame(CC = factor(1, levels = c(0,1)),
                       Online = factor(1, levels = c(0,1)))
#type="raw" -> class probs instead of label; [1,"1"] = p(loan=1)
PtG_prob <- predict(PtG_model, PtG_cust, type = "raw")[1, "1"]
round(PtG_prob, 4)
#compare all three estimates
round(c(B = PtB_prob, E = PtE_prob, G = PtG_prob), 4)
```

naiveBayes() gives P(Loan=1 | CC=1, Online=1) = `r round(PtG_prob, 4)`
the same as Part E (`r round(PtE_prob, 4)`).
Same math as Part E: the product of the conditional probabilities and the prior
for each loan class, divided by the sum over both classes.
